title: The history of Ayurveda
tagline: About 3,000 years from healing hymns and palm-leaf texts to a ministry, a WHO centre and fair trials.
intro: Ayurveda grew out of healing hymns, wandering physicians and Buddhist monasteries, and was written down in great Sanskrit compilations about 2,000 years ago. Physicians copied, argued over and added to those texts for centuries, and carried them to Baghdad, Central Asia and Europe. Colonial rule pushed it to the margins; Indian vaidyas, colleges and later the government revived it. In the 20th century one of its plants gave the world a blood-pressure drug, and scientists began asking the same question of the rest: what works, and is it safe?

eras.name: Hymns and wandering healers
eras.summary: Healing hymns in the Atharvaveda, and physicians around the early Buddhist monasteries. Dates are uncertain and debated.

eras.name: The great compilations
eras.summary: The Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas grow in layers, Vagbhata sums them up, and monastery universities teach medicine.

eras.name: Commentaries, recipes and travels
eras.summary: Translations in Baghdad, new texts on diagnosis, pulse and pharmacy, and Kerala physicians behind a famous European botany book.

eras.name: Decline and revival
eras.summary: Colonial rule favours Western medicine; vaidyas found pharmacies and colleges; a Kolkata kaviraj studies sarpagandha.

eras.name: A national system, put to the test
eras.summary: Reserpine, laws and regulators, the Ministry of AYUSH, safety studies, and a WHO centre in Jamnagar.

events.title: Healing hymns of the Atharvaveda
events.text: The Atharvaveda holds charms and hymns against fever, cough, wounds and snakebite, and names healing plants. Ayurveda calls itself an upaveda, an offshoot, of the Vedas. Its dates are uncertain, and historians see Ayurveda’s later, systematic ideas as coming from many sources.
events.why: It is the oldest Indian text with a large body of healing lore.

events.date: c. 5th century BCE (from later Buddhist texts)
events.title: Jivaka, physician to the Buddha
events.text: Buddhist texts tell of Jivaka, who studied medicine for seven years at Takshashila and became physician to the Buddha and King Bimbisara. The stories were written down centuries later, so they are legend as much as history.
events.why: They show that physicians trained with teachers and cared for monks in the Buddha’s time.

events.title: Ashoka plants medicinal herbs
events.text: Ashoka’s second rock edict says he arranged medical care for people and for animals, and had medicinal herbs, roots and fruit planted and brought in where they did not grow.
events.why: It is one of the earliest records of a state providing medical care.

events.date: compiled c. 100 BCE–200 CE; revised by Dridhabala c. 5th–6th century CE
events.title: The Charaka Samhita
events.who: Attributed to Charaka, after Agnivesha; completed by Dridhabala
events.text: The great text of internal medicine: 120 chapters on the three doshas, diet, diagnosis, medicines and the qualities of a good physician. It was compiled in layers, and the version we read today includes a later revision.
events.why: It set out the ideas that Ayurveda still teaches, from tridosha to prakriti.

events.date: layers from the last centuries BCE, completed c. 300–500 CE
events.title: The Sushruta Samhita and early surgery
events.text: A surgical text of 186 chapters. It describes over a hundred instruments, has students practise cuts on gourds and dead animals, and gives the first written account of rebuilding a nose with a flap of skin from the cheek.
events.why: Its rhinoplasty method is still recognised in the history of plastic surgery.

events.title: Monastery universities teach medicine
events.text: Nalanda grew into a great Buddhist centre of learning from about the 5th century. Visiting Chinese monks, among them Yijing in the 7th century, wrote about the medicine they saw practised in India; medicine was one of the subjects studied, though the details are uncertain.
events.why: Monasteries helped carry Indian medicine along the Silk Road to Central Asia, Tibet and China.

events.title: The Bower Manuscript
events.who: Found by Lt Hamilton Bower; read by Rudolf Hoernle
events.text: Birch-bark pages buried in a Buddhist stupa on the Silk Road hold Sanskrit medical texts, including a manual called the Navanitaka and a treatise on garlic. Hoernle, working in Calcutta, deciphered them between 1893 and 1912.
events.why: It is among the oldest surviving physical manuscripts of Indian medicine.

events.title: Vagbhata’s Ashtanga Hridaya
events.text: Vagbhata combined the teachings of Charaka and Sushruta into one clear text in verse, organised around the eight branches. It became the main textbook in Kerala and was translated into Tibetan.
events.why: It is still one of the most studied Ayurvedic texts today.

events.title: A book of diagnosis
events.text: The Madhava Nidana gathered the signs and causes of diseases, chapter by chapter, into one book on diagnosis (nidana). Later physicians used it as the standard reference.
events.why: It made diagnosis a subject of its own in Ayurveda.

events.title: Charaka and Sushruta in Arabic
events.text: At the Abbasid court, the Sushruta Samhita was translated into Arabic as the Kitab Shah Shun al-Hindi, and Charaka’s text was translated too. Indian physicians worked in Baghdad’s hospitals.
events.why: Indian medicine fed into the Greek-Arabic tradition that became Unani medicine (see UnaniClear).

events.title: The pulse enters the texts
events.text: The Sharangadhara Samhita standardised recipes for powders, decoctions and pills, and gave the earliest clear account of nadi pariksha, reading the pulse. Charaka and Sushruta do not describe pulse diagnosis as a method.
events.why: Pulse reading, now seen as typical of Ayurveda, is a later addition.

events.title: New plants and a new disease
events.text: The Bhavaprakasha added plants that had recently arrived in India and described phiranga roga, the “Frankish disease” (syphilis), brought by European sailors.
events.why: It shows Ayurveda changing to meet new plants and new diseases.

events.title: Kerala physicians behind Hortus Malabaricus
events.who: Itty Achuden, with Hendrik van Rheede
events.text: The Ezhava physician Itty Achuden dictated in Malayalam what his family’s palm-leaf manuscripts said about the plants of Malabar, checked by the Konkani physicians Ranga Bhat, Vinayaka Pandit and Appu Bhat. The Dutch governor van Rheede had it published with 794 copper engravings.
events.why: Indian healers’ plant knowledge became a founding book of tropical botany.

events.title: Colonial rule closes the Ayurveda classes
events.text: The Native Medical Institution (1822) had taught Ayurveda at the Sanskrit College and Unani at the Madrasa alongside Western medicine. A government order ended these classes, and the new Medical College taught only Western medicine.
events.why: For the next century Ayurveda survived outside official support, in families, pathshalas and pharmacies.

events.title: Revival: the Arya Vaidya Sala
events.text: P. S. Varier opened a small clinic and pharmacy that grew into one of India’s largest Ayurvedic hospitals and medicine makers. Across India, vaidyas founded colleges and associations to revive the system.
events.why: Standard, factory-made medicines and colleges shaped modern Ayurveda.

events.title: A kaviraj studies sarpagandha
events.who: Gananath Sen and Kartick Chandra Bose
events.text: The Ayurvedic physician Gananath Sen and the doctor Kartick Chandra Bose reported that powdered Rauvolfia serpentina root calmed disturbed patients and lowered blood pressure. The same year the chemist Salimuzzaman Siddiqui isolated its first alkaloids.
events.why: It started the path from a traditional herb to a modern drug.

events.title: Vakil’s trial in Mumbai
events.text: The cardiologist R. J. Vakil published a study of 50 patients with high blood pressure given Rauwolfia tablets for four weeks in the British Heart Journal. Most had a clear fall in blood pressure.
events.why: Often called the first clinical trial from India, it caught the world’s attention.

events.title: Reserpine is isolated
events.who: Johannes Müller, Emil Schlittler and Hugo Bein, Ciba
events.text: Chemists isolated the pure alkaloid reserpine from the root. It became one of the first modern drugs for high blood pressure and for severe mental illness. Its side effects, including depression, later made it rare.
events.why: Reserpine research helped Arvid Carlsson show dopamine’s role in the brain, work that won the 2000 Nobel Prize.

events.title: The Indian Medicine Central Council Act
events.text: The Act created the Central Council of Indian Medicine to set standards for Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani education and to keep a central register of qualified practitioners.
events.why: It made BAMS a regulated degree with national standards.

events.title: A research council for Ayurveda
events.text: The Central Council for Research in Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy (1969) split into separate councils. The Ayurveda one became today’s CCRAS, which runs clinical studies, drug standards and plant surveys.
events.why: It gave Ayurveda a national research body.

events.title: A government department, then AYUSH
events.who: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
events.text: India created a Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy in 1995. In 2003 it was renamed AYUSH, for Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy.
events.why: Traditional systems got a dedicated place in national health policy.

events.title: Heavy metals found in some products
events.text: Tests found potentially harmful lead, mercury or arsenic in 14 of 70 Ayurvedic products from Boston shops. A 2008 study of 193 products sold online found metals in about 1 in 5, and in about 4 in 10 metal-based rasa shastra products.
events.why: It made product safety a global concern.

events.title: Heavy-metal tests for exports
events.text: India ordered that every batch of Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani medicine made for export be tested for heavy metals, with results within set limits.
events.why: It was one of the first safety rules aimed at metal contamination.

events.title: The Ministry of AYUSH
events.text: The AYUSH department became a full ministry, with research councils for Ayurveda (CCRAS), Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy and Yoga and Naturopathy.
events.why: Ayurveda gained a full ministry, a rare status for a traditional system.

events.title: The first National Ayurveda Day
events.text: Ayurveda Day is held on Dhanvantari Jayanti. The first one focused on diabetes, and in 2017 the All India Institute of Ayurveda in New Delhi was dedicated to the nation on the same day.
events.why: It gave Ayurveda a yearly national spotlight and a flagship institute.

events.title: Reporting side effects of AYUSH medicines
events.who: Ministry of AYUSH, with AIIA as national centre
events.text: A national pharmacovigilance programme began collecting reports of side effects from AYUSH medicines and watching for misleading advertisements.
events.why: Safety monitoring is how rare harms are found.

events.title: NCISM replaces the old council
events.text: The National Commission for Indian System of Medicine Act replaced the Central Council of Indian Medicine with a new regulator for education and practice, including a national exit test for new graduates.
events.why: It modernised how Ayurvedic doctors are trained and registered.

events.title: A WHO centre in Jamnagar
events.who: WHO and the Government of India
events.text: The World Health Organization and India agreed to set up the WHO Global Centre for Traditional Medicine, backed by US$250 million from India, to study traditional medicine from around the world with modern science.
events.why: The first global WHO centre for traditional medicine puts evidence and safety at its heart.

events.title: Half of India uses AYUSH
events.text: The first all-India survey on AYUSH, of over 1.8 lakh households, found that about 46% of rural and 53% of urban people had used AYUSH to prevent or treat illness in the past year. Ayurveda was the most used.
events.why: It shows how many Indian families rely on these systems, which is why fair tests and safety matter.

facts: Ayurveda means “knowledge of life”, from ayus (life) and veda (knowledge).
The Sushruta Samhita has surgery students practise on gourds, melons and dead animals before touching a patient.
Pulse reading, now seen as typical of Ayurveda, first appears clearly around the 13th century, over a thousand years after Charaka.
Reserpine from sarpagandha helped reveal how dopamine works in the brain, research that won the 2000 Nobel Prize.
In a 2022–23 national survey, about half of Indians said they had used an AYUSH system in the past year.
